title: A third vote for tightening while domestic inflation continues to ease
summary: The July MPC voted 6–3 to keep Bank Rate at 3.75%. Catherine Mann joined Megan Greene and Huw Pill in seeking a rise to 4%. The change in voting matters because all members acknowledged that UK disinflation had continued before the latest energy shock and saw little evidence of persistent feedback so far. What differed was the weight placed on those observations. A benign data release is informative about prices already set. Its value for predicting wage settlements months away depends on how quickly firms and households adjust to renewed disruption (minutes, paragraphs 3–8 and 14–18).

The latest headline reading was June’s 2.6% annual CPI inflation. Motor fuel contributed 0.6 percentage points, while moderation in services and food prices helped bring the overall rate down. On 28 July front-month Brent was $84 a barrel and UK natural gas was 136 pence per therm. Strategic reserve releases and substitution among fuels had dampened crude prices. These measures offered less protection for gas and refined products, where supply was constrained. All members saw more upside than downside risk around the energy paths, even as most saw less scope for the extremes considered in April. Repeated episodes of disruption could prolong expensive household energy without recreating the same crude-oil peak (paragraphs 3–5).

The committee drew a practical distinction between three ways energy could reach the price index. The direct contribution of motor fuel was already measured. If a producer buys more expensive fuel and eventually raises its selling price, that gives a further, indirect contribution. More persistent inflation would require changes in how firms and households set prices or bargain over pay, capable of continuing after the original cost stops rising. These processes can overlap in the data. Someone surveyed about next year’s inflation can accurately anticipate higher energy bills while making no adjustment to the pay they expect to negotiate. A motor-fuel contribution cannot simply be subtracted from headline CPI to produce a measure of underlying domestic inflation (paragraphs 3–8).

The central projection used average energy-price paths over 15 days to 20 July and allowed moderate additional second-round effects. The adverse alternative featured renewed conflict, expensive energy for longer and much stronger domestic propagation. The milder path combined a more lasting de-escalation, lower energy prices similar to those in early July, no additional second-round effects and weaker household consumption. That last assumption matters. A difference in forecast inflation between these cases reflects both the original cost shock and what consumers and firms do afterwards. No common probability distribution over these paths was published in the minutes (paragraphs 9–12).

The timing of the information also mattered. The late-July front-month contracts described conditions after the end of the averaging period used in the projection. Members considered the possibility of repeated interruptions to shipping and refining, with European gas stocks below usual levels. Bailey highlighted both those exposures. Greene observed that some business surveys included responses from periods of a peace deal and renewed conflict. Averaging those responses can disguise how sharply an individual respondent revised their expectations. A monthly change in sentiment therefore offered an imperfect comparison with the daily energy-price news reaching the committee (paragraphs 3–4, 10 and members’ views).

Members had additional cross-checks beyond oil prices. Slower wages and softer labour demand supported further disinflation. Recent indicators of household expectations, firms’ own-price intentions, food prices and wage-price feedback offered little evidence of a persistent disturbance. For members such as Breeden, a more granular inflation indicator and money data added reassurance. For others, the observation window was too short, particularly for 2027 settlements. Global costs could also compound the energy shock through AI hardware bottlenecks or weather-related food prices, while trade diversion could exert downward pressure. These were risks affecting particular goods. The committee did not claim they were already jointly raising the broad price level (paragraphs 5–10 and individual statements).

Two separate judgements underpinned the interest-rate choice. The first was how restrictive borrowing conditions already were. An upward-sloping market curve and higher business and household financing costs could reduce demand even while the overnight rate stayed at 3.75%. The second was how much insurance to buy against more persistent price-setting. A rise could both make credit dearer and signal that monetary policy would react to repeated price shocks. The cost would fall on an economy with subdued demand, making an unnecessary rise harder to justify for members who feared long-lasting damage to employment. The level of Bank Rate by itself measures neither the total restraint on spending nor the value members placed on insurance (paragraphs 11–17).

Within the majority, Bailey thought that continued domestic disinflation might mean underlying persistence had previously been overstated. Breeden found support in detailed prices and money growth, while remaining concerned that climate, technology and energy supply disruptions could reinforce one another. Lombardelli thought subdued pricing power and a weaker labour market afforded time, but would respond if high energy prices themselves made feedback materially more likely. Dhingra saw cost pressure concentrated upstream, with vacancies below their pre-pandemic level and little amplification through margins. Waiting, in her view, would reveal more about first-round costs and next year’s settlements while still leaving time to react. Their agreement on the rate thus covered different thresholds for action (members’ views, pp. 5–6).

Ramsden thought inflation would probably have returned to target without the conflict. He explicitly envisaged either an increase if international pressures took hold or renewed cuts if they subsided. Taylor put the more likely outcomes between the central and milder cases, while allowing a long tail of inflationary outcomes. He emphasised the threat from deficient demand, weak private spending and possible damage to the labour market over the following year or two. In both accounts, holding long enough for financial conditions to remain restrictive could be an active policy choice relative to the easing path envisaged before the shock. Neither member promised a later cut (members’ views, pp. 6–7).

For Mann, the collapse of the US–Iran understanding and widening conflict provided evidence for the intermittent disruption she had considered in June. She saw a risk that repeated conspicuous price increases would lift expectations and ratchet up later price decisions. Greene also saw relatively benign current data, but judged an unnecessary early increase easier to reverse than a delay that allowed inflation to persist. Pill identified a different route to persistence. Even with long-term expectations still anchored and little sign of excess money growth, firms rebuilding margins and workers recouping purchasing power could influence one another’s decisions over several rounds. These distinct arguments led all three to favour 4% (members’ views, pp. 7–8).

For an event study, the information in this release includes the rate itself and an additional vote for a rise. The revised projection appeared at the same time. The committee judged the distribution of inflation risks tilted upwards and nevertheless maintained the rate. No post-announcement asset returns appear in the minutes. The reported £491 billion of government bonds held for monetary policy purposes was a stock measured on 17 July. It supplies balance-sheet context, without an accompanying vote on a new purchase or sale programme at this meeting (paragraphs 10–19).

questions.question: Was the absence of broader price increases in June genuinely informative about future wage-setting?
questions.detail: Construct a real-time indicator for price-change breadth outside fuel, utilities and food, then compare it with firms’ energy-contract expiry dates and the timing of pay negotiations. Look for later acceleration among previously insulated firms as contracts reset. A broad rise preceding those resets would point to expectations or demand. Changes concentrated at renewal would offer stronger evidence of delayed direct cost transmission.

questions.question: Do repeated energy shocks matter beyond their cumulative price change?
questions.detail: Compare episodes with similar average changes in sterling fuel and gas prices but different numbers of reversals and salient price increases. Test whether firms’ price plans or household expectations react more in the volatile episodes after allowing for labour-market slack and starting inflation. Use survey interview dates because the minutes note that responses collected on different sides of a geopolitical development can produce a misleading average.

questions.question: If borrowing conditions tightened before the vote, which households actually experienced that restraint?
questions.detail: Match fixed-rate mortgage resets to household spending and debt-service changes. Compare households with similar debt and income but different scheduled refinancing dates, while allowing for households’ direct energy exposure. A rise in quoted mortgage rates before the meeting can affect expectations immediately. Cash payments on existing fixed loans change on a different schedule, which matters for how rapidly demand can restrain prices.

questions.question: Did the change in voting alter expectations for the next meeting or primarily the distribution of risks?
questions.detail: Reconstruct expected vote counts and overnight rates just before the combined release. Inspect the change in meeting-dated forwards alongside options measuring asymmetry where prices are available. Flag the simultaneous projection and any energy headlines. A stronger price for protection against large hikes alongside little change in the most likely rate would be consistent with the insurance argument made by dissenters.
